title: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE
paragraphs: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE

The strange detail in 2 Chronicles 24:2–3 is not really a story about two wives. Read what happens after the man who guided Joash dies, and suddenly this becomes one of the most disturbing warnings in Scripture about borrowed faith.
There is one sentence in the story of King Joash that is incredibly easy to read past.
“And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters.”
That is 2 Chronicles 24:3 in the King James Version.
It sounds almost like a footnote.
Joash became king.
Joash did what was right.
Jehoiada the priest arranged his marriages.
Joash had children.
Then the story moves on.
But it is sitting beside another sentence that should make us uncomfortable:
“And Joash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
All the days of Jehoiada.
Those words are going to matter.
Because Joash had something many people would dream of having.
He had a godly man who rescued him.
Protected him.
Counseled him.
Helped establish him.
Helped shape his home.
Helped direct his kingdom.
Helped him repair the house of God.
Jehoiada had been involved in Joash’s life almost from the beginning.
And according to 2 Chronicles 24:3, Jehoiada even took two wives for him.
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ יְהוֹיָדָע נָשִׁים שְׁתָּיִם וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת
Vayyissa-lo Yehoyada nashim shettayim, vayyóled banim uvanot.
In straightforward English:
“Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he fathered sons and daughters.”

The Hebrew does not tell us the names of these women here. It does not tell us their feelings about the arrangement. It does not give us enough information to construct a romance, a conspiracy, or some secret theological meaning behind the number two.
So we should not invent one.
The text simply tells us that Jehoiada was deeply involved in the establishment of Joash’s household.
But that raises a far more important question.
Who was this priest that had so much influence over a king?
To understand that, you have to remember what happened when Joash was a baby.
His grandmother Athaliah seized power after the death of her son Ahaziah.
And then came one of the darkest sentences in Judah’s royal history.
She attempted to destroy the royal family.
Imagine the palace.
Doors opening.
Servants running.
Whispers becoming screams.
A royal bloodline being hunted.
And somewhere inside that nightmare was an infant who had no idea people wanted him dead.
Joash.
He could not defend himself.
He could not command soldiers.
He could not negotiate.
He could not even understand what was happening.
He survived because someone hid him.
Jehosheba took the child Joash and concealed him from the slaughter.
Second Chronicles 22 tells us that he remained hidden with them in the house of God for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.
Six years.
While a murderous queen sat on the throne, the future king was growing in hiding.
Think about that.
Athaliah thought she had eliminated the threat.
But somewhere beyond her sight, God was preserving a child.
She had the palace.
God had the promise.
She had political power.
God had providence.
She appeared to control the future.
She did not.
Somebody reading this needs that.
Because there are seasons when evil looks frighteningly successful.
You look at what happened to your family.
What happened to your marriage.
What happened to your children.
What somebody did to you.
What addiction stole.
What betrayal destroyed.
What your own sin nearly ruined.
And you wonder whether anything holy could possibly survive the wreckage.
Joash’s earliest story whispers back:
You do not know what God is preserving while darkness thinks it has won.
Eventually Jehoiada acted.
He gathered leaders.
He organized protection around the young heir.
He brought Joash out.
The crown was placed upon his head.
The testimony was given to him.
He was anointed.
And the people cried:
“God save the king.”
The boy who had once been hidden from execution was now sitting on the throne.
That is already a story of astonishing providence.
And Jehoiada remained beside him.
Second Chronicles 24 opens by telling us Joash was only seven years old when he became king.
Seven.
So picture the relationship.
This was not simply a king occasionally consulting a priest.
Joash grew into kingship under Jehoiada’s enormous influence.
The priest had helped save his life.
The priest helped secure his throne.
The priest guided him spiritually.
And eventually Scripture tells us:
“Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Then immediately:
“Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.”
There is something deeply human about this scene.
A rescued boy becomes a king.
The king becomes a husband.
The husband becomes a father.
Life begins replacing the terror of childhood.
A family grows where murder once threatened to erase a family line.
And yes, the text plainly says Joash had two wives.
We should neither hide that nor pretend that every action recorded in the Old Testament is automatically presented as God’s ideal.
The Bible frequently reports human behavior without commanding Christians to reproduce it.

From the beginning, Scripture’s foundational marriage pattern is expressed in Genesis 2:24 as a man being joined to his wife and the two becoming one flesh. Jesus Himself returned to that creation pattern in Matthew 19.
So 2 Chronicles 24:3 is narrative description, not a command establishing polygamy as the Christian model for marriage.
And perhaps surprisingly, Chronicles does not stop to condemn Jehoiada’s decision here.
That means we should be careful not to condemn more than the text condemns or approve more than the text approves.
Let Scripture speak.
But if you keep reading, the two wives stop being the most startling thing in the chapter.
Because something happens to Joash that is infinitely more frightening.
Jehoiada dies.
And suddenly we discover how much of Joash’s apparent spiritual stability had depended upon another man still being in the room.
Read the wording again.
Joash did right...
“all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Then Jehoiada died.
The man who had protected him was gone.
The voice that had guided him was silent.
The stabilizing presence disappeared.
And the officials of Judah came to Joash.
This time, Joash listened to them.
Second Chronicles 24:17–18 records the horrifying turn: after Jehoiada’s death, Judah’s officials influenced the king, the people abandoned the house of the LORD, and idolatry followed.
Stop there.
Because now this ancient king is standing frighteningly close to some of us.
You can live beside someone else's faith for years and mistake proximity to God for knowing God.
You can have praying parents.
A faithful pastor.
A godly spouse.
A grandmother who never stopped interceding.
A church that carried you.
A mentor who answered your midnight calls.
A friend who dragged you back every time you started wandering.
And all of those people can be tremendous gifts from God.
But none of them can surrender your heart to Christ for you.
There comes a moment when borrowed conviction must become personal conviction.
Borrowed prayer must become personal prayer.
Borrowed worship must become personal worship.
Borrowed obedience must become personal obedience.
Borrowed faith must become personal trust in God.
Joash apparently knew how to behave while Jehoiada was present.
But after Jehoiada was gone, another set of voices reached his heart.
That is terrifying.
Because the question is no longer merely:
Who influences you?
The deeper question is:
Who are you when your strongest spiritual influence leaves the room?
Who are you when your pastor cannot see you?
Who are you when your Christian friends are gone?
Who are you when nobody checks your browser history?
Who are you when your spouse is asleep?
Who are you when temptation knows your name and accountability is nowhere nearby?
Who are you when obeying Jesus costs something?
Maybe you have spent years looking like Joash during Jehoiada’s lifetime.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know what to post.
You know the worship songs.
You know the verses.
You know how Christians are supposed to sound.
But somewhere beneath all of that...
you know.
There is a room in your heart you have kept locked.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
An addiction you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it.
Bitterness you have fed for years.
Secret messages.
Secret lust.
Secret pride.
Secret jealousy.
Secret compromise.
A version of yourself nobody at church has ever met.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence a person can say is:
“I’m okay because I still look okay.”
Joash looked okay for years.
Then the supporting voice disappeared.
And what followed was devastating.
God did not immediately abandon the people to their rebellion.
He sent prophets to bring them back.
They refused to listen.
Then something almost unbearably tragic happened.
The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada.
Think about who this was.
The son of the man who had stood beside Joash.
The family of the priest who had helped preserve his throne.
Zechariah confronted the people with their disobedience.
And Joash—the child whose life had once been saved through Jehoiada’s household—ordered Jehoiada’s son killed.
He was stoned.
In the courtyard of the house of the LORD.
The rescued became complicit in destroying the son of his rescuer.
Scripture explicitly says Joash “remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him.”
How does a person travel that far?
How does a rescued child become that king?
Slowly.
That is usually how spiritual collapse happens.
Not always with one dramatic declaration that says, “I reject God.”
Sometimes it begins with listening to another voice.
Then tolerating another compromise.
Then ignoring another warning.
Then protecting another sin.
Until eventually the heart that once seemed tender can defend what it once would have wept over.
And this is where Joash stops being merely an ancient king.
He becomes a mirror.
Maybe your Jehoiada is still alive.
Maybe God has placed someone near you who keeps telling you the truth.
Your mother.
Your father.
Your pastor.
Your wife.
Your husband.
Your friend.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Someone who loves Jesus enough to make you uncomfortable.
Do not despise that voice.
But do not make that person your substitute for Christ either.
Because one day every earthly mentor disappears.
Every preacher eventually leaves the pulpit.
Every parent eventually releases the hand.
Every spiritual hero eventually dies.
And when every Jehoiada is gone, Jesus must still be enough.
That is where this story becomes Gospel.
Because if Joash’s story were only telling us to “be stronger,” we would eventually become another Joash.
Our deepest problem is not insufficient mentorship.
It is sin.
We need more than someone standing beside us.
We need Someone to save us.
We need more than improved behavior.
We need a new heart.
We need more than another Jehoiada.
We need Jesus Christ.
Joash was a king who was rescued from death and eventually wandered.
Jesus is the King who willingly entered death to rescue wanderers.
Joash received a crown after another family risked everything to preserve him.
Jesus wore a crown of thorns and gave Himself to preserve people who had rebelled against Him.
Joash forgot kindness shown to him.
Christ showed kindness to enemies.
Joash participated in the death of an innocent messenger.
Jesus—the truly innocent One—allowed sinful men to crucify Him and prayed for forgiveness for His executioners.
Joash needed grace.
So do we.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people finally earned God's acceptance.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the sinless Son of God bore sin and rose victorious.
That means your secret does not have to become your ending.
Your pornography does not have to become your ending.
Your adultery does not have to become your ending.
Your bitterness does not have to become your ending.
Your pride does not have to become your ending.
Your years of pretending do not have to become your ending.
Your spiritual coldness does not have to become your ending.
But grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you into the light.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable with the chains He came to break.
Repent.
Not because you can repair yourself enough for God to love you.
Repent because Christ is merciful.
Come into the light.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop using Christian activity to hide spiritual emptiness.
Stop borrowing somebody else's relationship with Jesus.
Run to Christ yourself.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Let the Savior who receives sinners begin rewriting what sin tried to make permanent.
And if this is exposing something you have kept hidden, do not manufacture a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Then send this to someone.
Not because an algorithm needs another share.
Because somebody you love may be living on borrowed faith right now.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ still receives sinners.
There may come a night when the voices around you change and you need to remember the lesson Joash learned too late:
A godly person can guide your faith, but nobody can have faith in Christ for you.
And if Gospel Warrior has been one of those voices continually calling you back to Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and Jesus Christ, stay close.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the unbeliever you have quietly been praying for—to follow too.
And if you believe this work should continue reaching more people, you can help carry it.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not because giving money makes someone more loved by God.
Scripture says giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion; “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity really can support Gospel work.
If you decide freely and prayerfully that you want to stand with us:
Give Jesus your heart.
Money can support a ministry.
It cannot save a soul.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus saves.
And perhaps that is the final ache in Joash’s story.
A man can have a Jehoiada choose his household...
protect his throne...
teach him righteousness...
stand beside him...
and still reach a day when the question becomes:
Will I personally remain faithful to God when the man who carried me this far is gone?
Sooner or later, every borrowed faith reaches that question.
Your parents cannot answer it for you.
Your pastor cannot answer it for you.
Your spouse cannot answer it for you.
Gospel Warrior cannot answer it for you.
You must come to Christ.
And if you have wandered, come back.
If you have failed, come back.
If you have been pretending, come into the light.
If your story has become scandalous, do not assume Jesus has finished writing.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Thomas doubted and was met by the risen Christ.
Paul persecuted His church and became a herald of the Gospel.
The cross stands forever as proof that God does not redeem people because their histories are spotless.
He redeems sinners through Jesus Christ.
So maybe tonight is not the night your story ends.
Maybe it is the night you finally stop borrowing someone else's faith.
Maybe it is the night you whisper the name you should have called upon long ago.
Jesus.
Save me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
Keep my heart when every other voice disappears.
And years from now, when somebody asks what happened to the person you used to be, may the answer be simple:
Jesus happened.
Because the most frightening thing about Joash was not that he needed someone to guide him.
It was that when the guiding hand disappeared, it became painfully clear whose hand his heart had never fully learned to hold.
